What's Next for Nvidia?

What's Next for Nvidia?

科技产品 作者 zdw 热度 476 回复 580 2026/11/16 07:55
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned 33 years after he co-founded the company. What happens to a company when a visionary CEO is gone? Most often innovation dies and the company coasts for years on momentum and its brand. Rarely does it regain its former glory. That’s the danger facing Nvidia. Here’s what their board should be considering. Here’s why.
  • Jensen Huang reinvented Nvidia three times. In 2006 he launched CUDA, turning a graphics chip for PC gamers into a general-purpose computing platform – and funded it for years ahead of any revenue. In 2012, when researchers used Nvidia chips to win the ImageNet contest, he pointed the company to deep learning. In 2020, with the acquisition of Mellanox, Nvidia went from selling boards with GPUs to selling integrated racks that power AI datacenters. These were not just product transitions, but radical business model transitions; new channels, new customers and new markets. Nvidia pivoted from a vendor of graphics boards, to a software platform, and then to systems company. It’s hard to imagine a CEO focused on executing an existing business model funding CUDA through those years.

Jensen's strategy has been to stimulate demand and then own as big a chunk of it as you can. This is the strategy of GPGPUs and CUDA. Have developers go create new demand for your cards and then lock them in. And they did. Financially, the circular deals are similar. Getting into making ASIC inference chips, you don't own the demand and you're making a commodity so you can't lock people in.

Steve Jobs was completely unsentimental about obsoleting Apple's lineup with new products but that's because Steve Jobs's strategy was to be a ruthless fast follower. Just wait for the technology to catch up with a burgeoning product category and then come out with a product with way more polish and sensible UX than everyone else. That's great for consumer electronics but its not so great for Nvidia. There's a lot less value in "taste" and "polish" when it comes to a device that's going to sit in a data center for its whole life.

torginus 2026/11/16 19:12
I am surprised nobody caught up to CUDA. Back in the early 10s I wrote my thesis in OpenCL, and I picked it on a whim, tooling seemed about equal.

Since then, OpenCL fell off completely while the CUDA of today doesn't seem all that different to my cursory inspection. Also, I'm not sure how high-level a language modern CUDA is, considering that back then it was common wisdom that every uArch was so different that you could easily lose more than half of the performance if you didn't optimize for it, which often meant swapping out entire algorithms or changing how the data is laid out. This applied to moving between vendors and moving to newer generations from the same vendor. So programming CUDA was much more about trying to coax the compiler into generating the right sort of assembly.

Besides, my impression is that the kernels that run LLMs are a relatively small-ish (thousands of lines). Even with awful tooling, you can get a couple engineers to port the code to your architecture of choice, or nowadays, you can get the agents themselves to do it for you.

14113 2026/11/16 19:39
I think CUDA has the same advantage that Apple has: It's entirely in-house, and engineers only need to optimise for in-house hardware. That means that design decisions can be made that only make sense for NVIDIA hardware, rather than (with OpenCL) providing an API that can be implemented by a much broader range of hardware. That narrower focus means that a) the API can move more quickly as new GPU features are made available (did you know that OpenCL still doesn't have support for bindless images!?), and b) as the surface is smaller and more hardware-specific, it can be optimised and tuned more effectively.

The other answer is that NVIDIA's offering isn't really CUDA - it's the various libraries like cuBLAS, cuDNN, CUTLASS, etc that provide extremely high performance kernels for machine learning and other gpu-relevant tasks. That's where NVIDIA locks in customers, as producing such high-quality libraries is extremely hard (many of the kernels for cuBLAS are written in uarchitecture-specific asm), and they get to define the interface, which means that it's hard for engineers to write portable code.

For people working in electronics, this is absolutely nothing new. The electronics / hardware side of silicon valley (and the counter parts in Taiwan, South Korea, China, and to a lower extent in Japan) is a cut-throat highly volatile environment. Software, in comparison, is much... softer.

NVIDIA can lose to the new Compute-in-Memory startups, if one of them successfully partners with other hardware companies with solid experience in scaling up. CIM has been the main topic of pretty much all electronics conferences I have attended this year, and it is picking up quickly.

Their main moat is in the training side of the hardware, whose market is far more limited than the inference side.
